Orthologous genes such as resistance to dieldrin ( rdl ) represent a high level of conservation, facilitating the translation of knowledge from D. melanogaster to pest species. figures.label: FIGURE 1
figures.caption: Neuropeptides regulating functions specific to larval versus adult Drosophila . These eight functions or actions are broadly defined and were selected since they are clear‐cut stage‐specific. Note that the NPHs listed play roles additional to the ones given here in both stages (for details and references, see Tables 2 , 3 , 4 ). For acronyms, see the list of peptide acronyms.

figures.label: FIGURE 2
figures.caption: Neurosecretory cells (NSCs) in the brain of the larva and adult. (A) Overview. (B) The cerebral neuroendocrine system of larva (top; horizontal view) and adult (bottom; sagittal view). Insulin‐producing cells (IPC) of the median NSC group are used as an example. The IPCs have axon terminations (presumed release sites) in corpora allata (CA), corpora cardiaca (CC), and aorta in both stages. In adults, additional sites are found in the anterior midgut and crop. SEZ, subesophageal zone; VNC, ventral nerve cord. Note that in the larva the CC and CA are situated anteriorly in a ring‐shaped tissue called the ring gland (also containing the prothoracic gland, PTG), and in adults CC and CA are located in the anterior thorax, associated with the aorta and proventriculus (PV) of the gut. The lower scheme is redrawn from Nässel et al. ( 2013 ); the upper one is novel. (C) In the larval brain and subesophageal zone (SEZ), there are 56 peptidergic NSCs of 11 main types. In addition, there are 16 endocrine cells in the CC portion of the ring gland‐producing adipokinetic hormone (AKH; not shown). Further hormones (non‐peptidergic) are produced in the ring gland: juvenile hormone (JH) in the CA and ecdysone (Ecd) in the prothoracic gland. The brain NSCs express the following peptides: myosuppressin (DMS), insulin‐like peptide (DILP), diuretic hormone 31 (DH31), diuretic hormone 44 (DH44), ion transport peptide (ITP), corazonin (CRZ), capability (CAPA), Hugin pyrokinin (Hugin‐PK), prothoracicotropic hormone (PTTH), eclosion hormone (EH). The median NSCs (MNC) produce DILPs, DH44, and DMS. Other acronyms: LNC, lateral NSCs; VmNC, ventromedial NSCs; SNC, subesophageal NSCs. (D) In the adult brain, there are also 56 NSCs but of nine different types (see also 2F). The two EH and four PTTH‐producing NSCs are lost just after metamorphosis. There appear to be 18 DILP‐producing MNCs (IPCs) instead of the larval 14. The corpora cardiaca and its AKH‐producing cells are not shown here. (E) Some NSCs and other neurons are present in pharate adults and first days of adult life. Two sets are larval NSCs that survive metamorphosis, LNC PTTH and VmNC EH (McBrayer et al. 2007 ). The others DM EH , DI EH , and PDF‐Tri are peptidergic interneurons that produce EH and PDF and appear during metamorphosis but then undergo apoptosis in the adult (Horodyski et al. 1993 ; McNabb et al. 1997 ; Scott et al. 2020 ; Selcho et al. 2018 ). The NSC terminology and numerical data are based on (McKim et al. 2024 ). (F) Table providing details on the number of NSCs and their NPH expression. The primary peptides listed are the ones first discovered in the cells listed. The NPH colocalization shown is demonstrated in adults. This table is based on data from McKim et al. ( 2024 ).

figures.label: FIGURE 3
figures.caption: In adult flies, NPHs of NSCs are produced by additional cell types and also display multiple non‐hormonal functions. (A) The NSCs of the brain. Note that each of the LNC CRZ clusters shown here includes three NSCs and four interneurons. (B) Ion transport peptide is produced in LNCs (LNC ITP ) but also in clock neurons (5th‐LNv and LNd ITP ). (C) NPHs of NSCs are expressed by multiple cell/neuron types. Two cell types (LNC ITP and IPC) express additional peptides: sNPF, TK, LK, and DSK. Nutrient sensing refers to nutrient‐sensing cells. (D) NPHs of NSCs have multiple additional roles, many of which are non‐hormonal and based on release from different cell/neuron types (the colocalized peptides as in B). For references, see Table 6 . This figure is compiled from Nässel ( 2025 ). (B is originally from Gera et al. 2025 , with permission.)

figures.label: FIGURE 4
figures.caption: Classification of NSCs and efferent neurons in ventral nerve cord (VNC). (A) The major classes of NSCs and efferent neurons in thoracic (T1–T3) and abdominal (A1–A8) neuromeres, shown in the larval CNS. Note that in adults, the locations of the abdominal NSC cell bodies are not as distinct, and segmental and median‐lateral positions are hard to discern. Median NSCs (e.g., Tv and Va) have axons projecting dorsally (and medially) into perisympathetic organs (Tv) or transverse nerves (Va) in larvae and neurohaemal areas in adults. Lateral (L) NSCs (e.g., CCAP and ABLK) have axons that exit via lateral segmental nerves in larvae and fused lateral abdominal nerves in adults (note that axons of CCAP neurons exit on the contralateral side). Median posterior (MP) efferent neurons (e.g., abPDF) exit posteriorly toward the hindgut and/or reproductive tract via median abdominal nerves. Note that of these, an NSC role has only been shown for abPDF and possibly some of the ILP7 MP neurons (see text). Some of these efferents (listed in B) may directly act on the tissues that they innervate. (B) Peptidergic NSCs in an unfused abdominal ganglion of the moth Manduca sexta display a clear medial‐lateral organization. To support the division of Drosophila NSCs into lateral and median, an M. sexta abdominal ganglion is shown. These neurons are individually identifiable and have been assigned acronyms, L1–L4 for lateral and M1–M5 for median. Shown additionally are peptidergic motoneurons (MN1) and interneurons (IN‐704) as well as ventral unpaired median (VUM) neurons. Note that some of the NPHs shown here are colocalized in certain NSCs but shown here separately (e.g., in L3, L4 cells and others). The median NSCs send axons via the anterior median nerve to an anteriorly located transverse nerve perivisceral organ (PVO) and the lateral ones via nerve 2 (N2) to the posterior transverse nerve (and some additional release sites). The NPHs allatotropin and pheromone biosynthesis activating neuropeptide (PBAN) are not found in Drosophila (although PBAN is a pyrokinin‐like peptide). This figure is slightly altered from Nässel ( 1996 ), which in turn was based on data from N. T. Davis et al. ( 1993 ), Taghert and Truman ( 1982 ), and Veenstra et al. ( 1994 ). (C) Table listing the peptidergic NSCs and efferents of the VNC in Drosophila larvae and adults. There are thoracic and abdominal lateral (L) and median (M) neurons. In brackets (abdominal lateral), the neuromere distribution of cells is provided. Note that only a few of the NSC groups have been given names (Tv, Va, ABLK, abPDF, iag); the rest are listed after the primary peptide they produce (colocalized peptides were commonly discovered later). Note that in some cases, the peptide was not found (‐), in other cases not investigated (?). For peptide acronyms, see list. For literature references, see main text (see also Figure 5 ).

figures.label: FIGURE 5
figures.caption: Peptidergic NSCs in the larval and adult ventral nerve cord. (A–C) Larval NSCs. In thoracic neuromeres (T1–T3), only three pairs of FMRFamide‐producing NSCs have been identified (Tv neurons) and one pair of CCAP‐producing neurons. In abdominal neuromeres (A1–A8), NSCs are located segmentally laterally and more medially. Some of the NSCs have been assigned names (shown in bold font). The peptide acronyms are: diuretic hormone 31 (DH31) and 44 (DH44), capability (CAPA), glycoprotein hormone B (GBP5), leucokinin (LK), crustacean cardioactive peptide (CCAP). Note that the Va and Tv neurons send axons to the dorsal midline where they terminate in perisympathetic organs (Tv neurons) and dorsal transverse nerves (Va neurons); see Figure 6 . The lateral NSCs send axons through segmental nerves to body wall muscle. Note that the anterior ABLKs coexpress LK and DH44 (and octopamine), and the ones in A6 and A7 additionally express DH31 (Tsukasa et al. 2026 ; Zandawala et al. 2018 ). Note that it is not clear whether the abdominal CCAP neurons in C are the same as the bursicon/CCAP neurons in B. C1 and C2: Confocal images of CCAP‐expressing neurons in the VNC of the larva displayed with ccap ‐GAL4 (C1) and CCAP‐immunolabeling (C2) in the same specimen. The asterisks indicate the CCAP neurons in T3 and A1–A4 in 4C, which display stronger immunolabeling. Note that a pair of neurons in T3 (yellow asterisk) also has axons to the periphery like the ones in A1–4 (see Karsai et al. 2013 ; Vömel and Wegener 2007 ). (D and E) Adult NSCs. The same neuropeptides are produced in adults, but the numbers of NSCs differ in some cases from the larva (ABLKs, bursicon/CCAP and Orcokinin A neurons; Chen et al. 2015 ; de Haro et al. 2010 ; Luan et al. 2006 ; Sellami et al. 2011 ; Zandawala et al. 2018 ). Also, the co‐expression of peptides differs for the ABLK neurons, and the NPH of anterior Va1 neurons has not been determined in adults. Note that in adults, the Va and Tv neurons supply axon terminations to extensive neurohemal areas in the dorsal neural sheath of the ventral nerve cord (see Figure 6 ). The remaining neurons in A1–A8 send their axons via the lateral abdominal nerves (arrows) to peripheral targets.

figures.label: FIGURE 6
figures.caption: Release sites of larval and adult NSCs of the ventral nerve cord (VNC) change during metamorphosis. (A and B) Larval and adult Tv and Va neurons express FMRFamide and capability (CAPA), respectively (shown in dorsal view). In the larva, Tv neurons of thoracic neuromeres T1–T3 supply axon terminations to dorsal perisympathetic organs (tPSO; also known as neurohemal organs), whereas the adult Tv neurons supply axon terminations to a dorsal neurohemal plexus covering the VNC (see panels B–D). In larvae, the Va neurons of abdominal neuromeres A2–A4 send their axons dorsally into median transverse nerves (see also panel B). (B) Side view and transverse views of the VNC showing the tPSOs, transverse nerve, and dorsal neurohemal plexus. Note that in the side view, the abdominal transverse nerves are not shown. (C) Side view of the adult VNC with Tv neurons of thoracic neuromeres T1–T3 and Va neurons of A2–A4. Both neuron types send axons into the dorsal neural sheath where they arborize and form varicosities, as depicted in D (note that only the Tv neuron plexus is shown in D). (D) Dorsal view of the VNC with the thoracic neurohemal plexus. (E) Release sites of different types of NSCs (numbered 1–7). Release sites (axon terminations) are shown crosshatched in aorta, dorsal surface of VNC, and hindgut). The examples of NSCs shown here include a set of four serotonergic (5‐HT) neurons in the SEZ that send axons to the same neurohemal area as the FMRFamide‐producing Tv neurons. The posterior neurons (5, ITP and 6, LK) exit via median (M) or lateral (L) abdominal nerves, respectively, to innervate dorsal aorta (heart) and body wall muscles (L) and hindgut (M). Further acronyms: CC, corpora cardiaca; CA, corpora allata. RT, renal tubules (shown truncated). (A) and (B), original. (C) and (D) from Lundquist and Nässel ( 1990 ), (E) from Nässel ( 1996 ), all with permission.

figures.label: FIGURE 7
figures.caption: Posterior abdominal efferent neurons and NSCs that produce NPHs in larvae and adults. In both stages, sets of neurons in abdominal neuromeres send axons to the hindgut (and associated structures, e.g., rectal pads in adults) and in adults also to the reproductive tract (ILP7 neurons) via the median abdominal nerve(s). Some of these may serve as NSCs where the peptides have functions as circulating hormones (only shown for PDF and maybe ILP7), but the majority of the neurons seem to act locally on targeted tissues. (A and B). Larval neurons. Acronyms: AstA, allatostatin A; ITP, ion transport peptide; PDF, pigment‐dispersing factor; CCAP, crustacean cardioactive peptide; ILP7, insulin‐like peptide 7. Note that the two Dp7 neurons in B are not efferents but ascending interneurons that target the insulin‐producing cells (IPCs) in the brain (they are included for a function related to in the text). Note that a possible co‐expression of the peptides in A is possible, similar to adults, but needs to be confirmed. RYa, RYamide. (C and D) Adult efferents and NSCs that target hindgut and/or reproductive tissues. The PDF‐producing cells seem to release hormonal PDF that acts on Malpighian tubules (Talsma et al. 2012 ). The axons of these neurons exit via the median abdominal nerves (arrows). Acronyms as in (A and B). (E and F). A sex dimorphism has been demonstrated in the adult ILP7 neurons where embryo‐ and adult‐derived neurons exist. In males (E), the adult ILP7 neurons co‐express glutamate and serotonin (5‐HT) and innervate the seminal vesicle, the embryonic ones produce only ILP7 and innervate the hindgut. In females (F), two pairs of additional adult cells (yellow) co‐express ILP7 and glutamate, and they and another set of adult neurons innervate the reproductive tract (oviduct muscle), and the embryonic ones innervate the hindgut. Note that proctolin has also been detected in six efferent neurons in the VNC of larvae and adults (Anderson et al. 1988 ; Taylor et al. 2004 ) and innervate the hindgut musculature (Anderson et al. 1988 ) but are not shown here (maybe colocalization in the PDF neurons?).

figures.label: FIGURE 8
figures.caption: Peptidergic neurons that regulate ecdysis during development display other functions in adults. (A) A set of neurons in the brain, subesophageal zone (S1–3), and ventral nerve cord (T1–3 and A1–9) has been extensively investigated for its role in a cascade of events underlying the shedding of cuticle during stages of ecdysis and post‐ecdysis (shown in B). These neurons express the receptor of ecdysis‐triggering hormone (ETH), ETHR‐A, and produce EH, FMRFamide (FMRFa), crustacean cardioactive peptide (CCAP), LK myoinhibitory peptide (MIP), and bursicon (Burs). (B) ETH released from Inka cells (peritracheal cells), under ecdysone control, acts to regulate activity in the other peptidergic neurons that express ETHR‐A receptor. These neurons and their NPHs in turn influence motor activity and other functions during the ecdysis cascade to ensure timely shedding of cuticle and processes after ecdysis including glue expulsion to attach pupae and tanning of the cuticle. (C) Other functions of NPHs utilized by the same set of neurons in larvae and adults. (A and B) are originally based on Y. ‐J. Kim et al. ( 2006 ) but redrawn in Nässel and Zandawala ( 2019 ) and updated after Zitnan et al. ( 2026 ). For data and references in (C), see Tables 2 and 3 .

figures.label: FIGURE 9
figures.caption: A drastic expansion of the clock circuits is seen in the numbers of clock neurons and NPHs at the larval‐to‐adult transition in Drosophila . (A) The clock neurons in the larval brain. Only four types of clock neurons have been identified. (B) Larval clock neurons identified with a timeless ( tim )‐GAL4 driver. (C) Only PDF has been clearly demonstrated in larval clock neurons, whereas CCHa1 is likely present in DN1a neurons based on knockdown experiments (Acklin et al. 2026 ; Poe et al. 2024 ). In the 5th‐LNv, the peptide remains unknown (not shown in figure). (D) Adult clock neurons. The neurons encircled in blue are found both in larvae and adults (note that not all the neurons in the DN2 and DN3 clusters are shown). The LNv ITP are also known as 5th‐LNv. (E) The adult clock neurons from the clock connectome. Note that the colors of the neurons in this panel do not always correlate with those in (D). (F) The different NPHs in adult clock neurons (further peptides have been indicated by single ‐cell transcriptomics, Reinhard et al. 2024 , but need further confirmation). See the list of acronyms for the NPHs. (A) is redrawn from Wegener et al. ( 2026 ), (B) is from Hamasaka and Nässel ( 2006 ) with permission, (D) is redrawn from Reinhard et al. ( 2024 ), and (E) is from Reinhard et al. ( 2024 ; Nature Communications 15, 10392; open access).

figures.label: FIGURE 10
figures.caption: In adult flies, NPHs of clock neurons are also produced by other cell types. (A) Clock neurons in the adult Drosophila brain (from Reinhard et al. 2024 ), with permission, eLife , open access. The NPHs produced in the clock neurons are shown in red (peptide acronyms in list). (B) NPHs of clock neurons are produced by multiple other cell types. This figure is from Nässel ( 2025 ), with permission.

figures.label: FIGURE 11
figures.caption: Intestinal enteroendocrine cells (EECs) in larvae and adults of Drosophila . Note that the renal tubules are shown truncated in both stages. (A) The adult intestine and its complement of peptidergic EECs. Ten peptides (NPHs) have been identified (see acronyms in separate list) and are distributed in the five main regions of the midgut (1–5). One peptide, tachykinin (TK), is also found in EECs in the anterior hindgut (region 6; also shown in B). Note that the NPHs are distributed in different patterns in the different regions, and several are co‐expressed in the same EECs (not detailed here). (B) Immunolabeling with anti‐tachykinin (TK) and tk ‐GAL4 expression in the posterior midgut and anterior hindgut of adult Drosophila . (C) Larval EECs express the same NPHs but in slightly different distribution patterns, compared to adults, and one additional peptide, limostatin, was identified in the anterior midgut. The midgut is divided into anterior (AM), median (MM) and two posterior regions (PM‐A and PM‐C). The distribution of NPHs in EECs is shown schematically in the boxes where co‐expression patterns are indicated by the grouping of acronyms. One major difference is the very restricted distribution of TK in the larva, compared to the adult. No NPH has been identified in the larval hindgut. (A) is modified from Nässel and Zandawala ( 2022 ), (B) is from Liu, Luo, and Nässel ( 2016 ) with permission, (C) is redrawn from S. Jang et al. ( 2021 ).

figures.label: FIGURE 12
figures.caption: Neuropeptides/peptide hormones regulating nutrient sensing and/or food seeking and feeding in larval and adult Drosophila . Larval CNS (top) and adult brain (bottom) with brain and subesophageal zone (SEZ) neurons involved in nutrient sensing and/or feeding. Guide to NPHs located in brain and SEZ neurons is given in the box to the left. The peptides listed in the box to the right are located in cells outside the brain and SEZ (except for AKH, in the intestine), or in the case of AstA, it is not clear whether they are in cells of the brain or intestine. The peptides affecting feeding/nutrient sensing in both larvae and adults are indicated in blue font in the list with color‐coded cell bodies to the left. The brain neurons are insulin‐producing cells (IPC), dorsolateral neurons (DLP; also known as LNC CRZ ), Median NSCs‐producing DH44 (MNC DH44 ), two types of NPF interneurons (NPFa and b) and a cluster of Hugin cells (note that these are a heterogeneous group, including a pair of NSCs, SNC Hugin ). In the adult brain, several additional neurons are implicated CCAP, LHLK, MNC DMS , MP1, MP3, PLP, SIFa, SELK, and SNC CAPA . For references, see Tables 3 and 4 .

figures.label: FIGURE 13
figures.caption: Peptidergic pathways regulating larval and adult functions in Drosophila related to feeding, development, growth, and reproduction. The peptides shown alter their functions between larvae and adults, except their roles in the regulation of food seeking and feeding (indicated as feeding in the figure). Both in larvae and adults feeding depends on nutrient sensing in the fat body, gut endocrine cells, or some specific brain neurons. Also, growth, ovary maturation, and reproduction are nutrient‐dependent. Note that here reproduction refers to female flies. (A) In the larva, a set of peptidergic neurons form pathways that regulate developmental timing or growth, dependent on nutrient status (and nutrient sensing). These include the brain, subesophageal zone (SEZ), corpora allata, prothoracic gland, and midgut (and fat body, not shown). Feeding is regulated by neuropeptide F (NPF; Pu et al. 2018 ; Y. Wang et al. 2013 ), allatostatin A (AstA; C. Wang et al. 2012 ), and Hugin pyrokinin (Hugin; Schlegel et al. 2016 ) and furthermore by insulin‐like peptides (DILPs) released from insulin‐producing brain neurons (Colombani et al. 2005 ) to inhibit NPF neurons in fed larvae. The role of CRZ in feeding has not been determined in larvae. The same peptides regulate developmental growth and timing (including molts) via regulation of juvenile hormone (JH) and ecdysone production in corpora allata and prothoracic gland, respectively. The ecdysone production is regulated by PTTH and DILPs released from brain neurons (McBrayer et al. 2007 ). These PTTH neurons are activated by Hugin‐PK, CRZ, and AstA (Deveci et al. 2019 ; Imura et al. 2020 ; Ohhara et al. 2024 ). JH and ecdysone mutually inhibit each other's biosynthesis (S. Liu et al. 2018 ). DILPs have direct effects on nutrient‐dependent tissue growth (Colombani et al. 2005 ; Demontis and Perrimon 2010 ; Ikeya et al. 2002 ). (B) In the adult, most of the same peptides regulate feeding and reproduction (including sexual maturation). This figure shows female pathways. NPF, CRZ, and AstA and indirectly Hugin (via sugar sensing), regulate feeding (Hentze et al. 2015 ; Hergarden et al. 2012 ; Kubrak et al. 2016 ; Oh et al. 2021 ; Qin et al. 2025 ; Schwarz et al. 2021 ; Yoshinari et al. 2021 ). The CRZ neurons also affect feeding indirectly via DILPs by means of colocalized sNPF, indicated by * (Oh et al. 2019 ). NPF released from EECs of the midgut affects metabolism and aging indirectly via the DILP‐producing cells and JH (Chen et al. 2024 ) and follicle maturation in ovaries (not shown; Sadanandappa et al. 2021 ). In adults, there is no prothoracic gland, but in females, ecdysone is produced by the ovaries and regulates female reproduction by promoting biosynthesis of vitellogenin in the fat body (Swevers 2019 ; Zhu et al. 2021 ). In males, ecdysone is produced in the male accessory glands (not shown here; Hentze et al. 2013 ). DILPs regulate production of JH in corpora cardiaca (Tu et al. 2005 ), and DILPs and JH regulate female reproduction by promoting vitellogenesis in the fat body (LaFever and Drummond‐Barbosa 2005 ); and both hormones also affect aging (Chen et al. 2024 ). Note that the insulin‐producing cells that release DILPs receive multiple inputs from other neurons, mediating nutrient status and internal state (see Bisen et al. 2025 ; Nässel and Vanden Broeck 2016 ). Hugin neurons innervate the corpora allata, but their function is unknown (Mizuno et al. 2021 ). This figure is redrawn, from parts of a figure from Kay et al. ( 2025 ), with some alterations and updates.

figures.label: FIGURE 14
figures.caption: The metamorphosis of the mushroom bodies (MB) and its neuropeptides. The relatively simple larval MB has one major type of intrinsic neurons (γ Kenyon cells) and a few neuronal input and output compartments in the peduncle (Ped), horizontal and vertical lobes (gray boxes). The adult MB has three major types of intrinsic neurons (γ, αβ, and α‘β‘ Kenyon cells) that innervate specific compartments of the lobes (γ, β and γ lobes). This remodeling involves some pruning of larval neurons and addition of novel adult ones. The larval γ neurons regrow and form part of the adult circuitry (the adult γ cells innervate the γ1–γ5 compartments but no longer the vertical lobe). Images are redrawn and simplified from Truman et al. ( 2023 ). The bottom panels depict subsets of Kenyon cells producing short neuropeptide F (sNPF), the only known neuropeptide in the MB intrinsic neurons. In larvae, these are the majority of the γ neurons, whereas in adults, sNPF is expressed in subpopulations of γ, β, and γ Kenyon cells but not the α‘β‘ cells. These images are from Nässel et al. ( 2008 ) with permission.

figures.caption: Summary of samples included in the global UShER-TB phylogenomics resource. (a) Global phylogeny of 129,312 samples processed with the myco pipeline and placed with usher-sampled. The phylogeny, samples and metadata can be explored interactively on Taxonium . (b) Geographical distribution of samples. Note that sample depth does not necessarily correspond to density of infections, as sequencing resources contribute heavily to data collection.

figures.label: Fig. 3.
figures.caption: Motivation and effects of local masking. (a) Example demonstrating a placement artefact that occurs when samples have missing sequence information, where their close neighbours may have variants. On the left, Sample B has missing data (highlighted in the sequence alignment in orange) at position 6, while neighbours C and D share a >T mutation (mutations highlighted in blue) there. The placement algorithm treats this as a difference, inflating mutation distances despite alignment evidence. To avoid such false distances between closely related samples, we mask mutations like those at positions 6 and 8 (right) (see Methods). (b) To test the effect of multiple rounds of post-inference local masking, we tracked the number of mutations needing to be masked across four rounds of the procedure. (c) We tracked the number of revertant mutations present in the global tree after each round of masking to assess improvements in phylogenetic quality.

figures.label: Fig. 4.
figures.caption: Placement consistency in different settings. (a) Summary of transmission cluster assignment results in local and global settings. (b) Proportion of samples that are correctly assigned to their original transmission group. (c) Proportion of samples that fall within two or less nodes from their original location in the tree. In both cases, different scenarios are considered. From left to right: local dataset placing 40% of samples (LP_40), global dataset placing 40% of the samples (GP_40) and global dataset placing all the sequences (GP_all).

figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Examples of phalloidin‐labeled F‐actin fluorescence within in situ human chondrocytes. (A) represents high power magnification images (a–c) of in situ chondrocytes illustrating (a) cortical F‐actin, (b) tracing and measurement of average F‐actin fluorescence, using the Freehand selection (thin yellow broken line), and (c) intensity of F‐actin, using Freehand line tools in ImageJ. Examples of the intensity were shown in (c) as intense punctate (IP) and intense areas (IAs). Examples of cytoplasmic process/es (d) and (e), with the classification of F‐actin labeling localization (f), phalloidin‐labeling was assessed on a projected 3D image, highlighting the cortical ring associated with the cell membrane. Bar = 10 µm. Panel (B) shows the fluorescence profile along the cortical region in (a). The red line identified fluorescence levels around the cortical ring. figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Overview of the experimental workflow for dynamic microfluidic culture of human articular chondrocytes and induction of osteoarthritis‐like inflammation under gravity‐driven flow. Schematic representation of the integrated workflow comprising three basic protocols. Basic Protocol 1 : extracellular matrix (ECM) protein coating and equilibration of microfluidic chips. Basic Protocol 2 : harvesting, sequential seeding of human articular chondrocytes, and initiation of gravity‐driven bidirectional flow through asymmetric reservoir filling and rocker‐induced tilting, enabling dynamic culture for up to 21 days. Basic Protocol 3 : induction of OA‐like inflammation using IL‐1β (days 15–21), followed by downstream analyses at defined time points. Representative readouts include metabolic activity, secretion of ECM components, cytokines, and MMPs, and fluorescence imaging of cell viability, morphology, and ECM marker expression. Note: Some graphical elements were created using BioRender.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Microfluidic platform and chip layout for dynamic chondrocyte culture under gravity‐driven flow. (A) Photograph of the microfluidic chip with reservoirs filled with culture medium, illustrating the assembled device used for experiments. (B) Schematic representation of the microfluidic chip layout showing an array of 24 culture units. Each unit comprises two culture medium reservoirs connected by four microchannels with varying width and height, subdivided into regions I–III to generate spatial gradients of fluid shear stress under gravity‐driven flow conditions.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Proper pipette handling for liquid injection, loading, and extraction in microfluidic culture units. Schematic representation of recommended pipette handling techniques for introducing and removing liquids in microfluidic chips. Injection of coating solution and cell suspension: The pipette tip should gently contact the inlet aperture at the bottom of the reservoir without insertion into the channel inlet, followed by slow injection to allow smooth flow through the microchannels toward the opposite reservoir. Direct insertion of the pipette tip into the inlet should be avoided to prevent damage to the channel structure and leakage. Liquid loading (culture medium, DPBS, assay solutions): Add liquids directly to the reservoirs without contacting the inlet apertures. Direct injections into the channel inlet should be avoided to prevent flow disruption and the introduction of air bubbles. Liquid extraction: Liquids should be removed from the reservoirs without contacting the inlet apertures to ensure that the microchannels remain filled. Aspiration from the microchannels should be avoided to prevent bubble formation and loss of fluid continuity within the system. Correct handling is indicated by green check symbols, while incorrect procedures are indicated by red crosses.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Workflow for experimental determination of gravity‐driven flow rate in microfluidic chips under rocker‐induced tilt. Schematic overview of the experimental procedure used to measure flow rates during the dwell period at a defined tilt angle (±25°). (1–2) Microfluidic chips are coated with extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins (fibronectin‐collagen type IV mixture) and equilibrated with culture medium under incubator conditions. (3) Collection vials are pre‐weighed using an analytical balance prior to flow measurements. (4) Reservoirs are asymmetrically filled (e.g., 100 µl vs. 50 µl) to establish a hydrostatic pressure difference driving fluid flow between reservoirs. (5) The chip is placed on a rocker platform at room temperature and operated under defined conditions (±25° tilt, 1 rpm, 300 sec dwell period). The dwell period begins at the maximum tilt position (25°) and is defined at t = 0 sec. (6) During the 300‐sec dwell period, the cumulative transferred volume to the initially lower‐volume reservoir is collected at defined time points (e.g., 60, 120, 180, and 240 sec) using pre‐weighed vials. For each time point, independent microfluidic units are used. The collected volumes are determined by gravimetric measurement. (7) Measurements are repeated across five independent culture units per sampling time point. Transferred volumes and flow rates are calculated as Δ V i = V i − V i −1 and Q i = Δ V i /Δ t , and plotted as a function of time. Note: Graphs are reproduced from da Silva et al. ( 2026 ) licensed under CC BY 3.0.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Image processing workflow for z‐stack analysis and fluorescence quantification in Fiji (ImageJ). Screenshots illustrate key steps in image processing and preparation for extracellular matrix (ECM) marker quantification. Panels show representative Fiji (ImageJ) interfaces for: visualization of z‐stack images with merged fluorescence channels (collagen type II, green; aggrecan, red; DAPI, blue); generated z‐projection images with merged channels (Scale bar = 100 µm); individual z‐stacks for each fluorescence channel separately; Fiji (ImageJ) toolbar; and the Brightness & Contrast (B&C) adjustment window. Displayed z‐stack images correspond to a single optical slice (typically the first slice) within the stack. Navigation through the full z‐stack is performed using the scroll bar or arrow controls in the Fiji (ImageJ) interface. Lookup tables (LUTs) are assigned to each channel for visualization purposes only and do not modify the underlying grayscale intensity values. Brightness and contrast may be adjusted to facilitate visualization and accurate ROI selection. However, the “Apply” function should not be used, as it permanently alters pixel intensity values and compromises quantitative fluorescence analysis.

figures.label: Figure 6.
figures.caption: Image processing workflow for ROI selection and fluorescence quantification in Fiji (ImageJ). Screenshots illustrating key steps for ROI selection and fluorescence quantification in Fiji (ImageJ). Representative images show individual fluorescence channels (collagen type II, green; aggrecan, red) from z‐stack data. Displayed images correspond to the first slice of the z‐stack; navigation through slices is performed using the scroll bar or arrow controls in the Fiji (ImageJ) interface. The ROI Manager interface (Analyze → Tools → ROI Manager) was used to define measurement regions. Individual cells were manually selected in the first channel using the freehand selection tool and assigned as ROIs (yellow outlines, labeled 1‐6), then added to the ROI Manager. Additional background ROIs (n = 5) were defined outside the microchannels using square selections and added to the same ROI set. ROIs were subsequently overlaid onto the second channel using the “Show all” function to ensure consistent measurement across channels. Measurement parameters were defined in the Set Measurements menu (Analyze → Set Measurements), and fluorescence intensity values (gray values), integrated density, and area were obtained by selecting each channel and applying the “Measure” function in the ROI Manager.

figures.caption: Workflow for ELISA‐based quantification of secreted inflammatory and extracellular matrix (ECM) markers. (B) Multiplex ELISA (Q‑PLEX) workflow for quantification of inflammatory mediators (MMPs and cytokines), including sample dilution, plate loading, chemiluminescence detection, and data analysis using calibration curves. (C) Standard ELISA workflow for quantification of collagen type II fragments, including sample dilution, absorbance measurement (450 ± 10 nm), and concentration determination by interpolation.

figures.caption: Expected cellular responses of human articular chondrocytes under dynamic culture and IL‑1β‐induced inflammatory conditions. (A) Representative z‐projection fluorescence images of chondrocytes cultured for 21 days in microchannels coated with a fibronectin–collagen type IV mixture. (B) Representative Live/Dead fluorescence images showing time‐dependent viability and proliferation of chondrocytes cultured under dynamic conditions on days 3, 7, 14, and 21 (control), compared with IL‑1β‐stimulated cultures on day 21 (1 and 10 ng/ml, applied from day 15 to day 21). (C) Representative z‐projection immunofluorescence images of ECM marker expression in region I after 21 days of culture, comparing control and IL‑1β‐stimulated samples. Images show merged fluorescence channels for collagen type II (green), aggrecan (red), and nuclei (DAPI, blue). (D–E) Quantification of corrected total cell fluorescence (CTCF) for collagen type II (D) and aggrecan (E) across regions I–III for control and IL‑1β‐stimulated cultures at day 21 (n = 44 cells per group). (F) Cell metabolic activity measured using a PrestoBlue assay for control and IL‑1β‐stimulated samples at day 21 ( n = 5 independent samples per group). (G–H) Quantification of inflammatory mediators in culture supernatant collected at day 21 using multiplex ELISA, including matrix metalloproteinases (MMP‐1, MMP‐2, MMP‐3, MMP‐7, MMP‐9, MMP‐13) and cytokines (IL‑1β, IL‑6, IL‑8) ( n = 3 independent samples per group). figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Separate (S‐type) versus linked (L‐type) organization of 35S and 5S rDNA units. (a) Schematic representation of the separate arrangement (S‐type), in which tandem arrays of 5S rDNA (5S rRNA gene + non‐transcribed spacer, NTS) and 35S rDNA (18S–ITS1–5.8S–ITS2–26S + intergenic spacer, IGS) occur as independent repeats (monomers). (b) Representative RepeatExplorer graph‐based reconstruction for an S‐type species ( Tragopogon dubius ), showing the main rDNA clusters: a 35S rDNA path (with annotated 18S, ITS1, 5.8S, ITS2, 26S and IGS regions) and a separate 5S rDNA cluster constituted by the 5S gene and NTS. (c) Dual‐color FISH examples consistent with the S‐type arrangement (left: Tragopogon mirus ; right: Helianthus annuus ), showing 35S and 5S rDNA signals at distinct chromosomal/nuclear sites (reprinted from Garcia et al., 2010 , with permission). (d) Schematic representation of the linked arrangement (L‐type), where 35S and 5S rDNA are physically linked within the same tandemly repeated unit (35S–IGS1–5S–IGS2), defining a single composite monomer. (e) Representative RepeatExplorer graph‐based reconstruction for an L‐type species ( Artemisia annua ), showing a single linked cluster that contains both 35S and 5S regions within the same repeat, separated by two IGS segments (IGS1 and IGS2). (f) Dual‐color FISH examples consistent with the L‐type arrangement (left: Artemisia tridentata ; right: Tagetes patula ), showing predominantly co‐localized or closely overlapping 35S and 5S signals (overlap visible as yellow‐orange). In (c, f), chromosomes/nuclei are counterstained with DAPI (blue); 35S and 5S rDNA signals are shown in green and red, respectively (overlap = orange). Scale bars as indicated. Reproduced from Garcia et al. ( 2009 ) Chromosoma 118:85–97 and from Garcia et al. ( 2010 ) BMC Plant Biology 10:176, licensed under CC BY 2.0.
